parsed_answer.content:
A PriorityQueue in Java is an unbounded priority queue based on a priority heap data structure. Unlike standard first-in, first-out (FIFO) queues that process elements strictly based on their insertion order, a PriorityQueue orders its elements according to their natural ordering or by a custom Comparator provided at construction time. This makes it an indispensable collection for algorithms like Dijkstra's shortest path, A* search, Huffman coding, and greedy scheduling problems where access to the minimum (or maximum) element must be efficient.

The underlying binary heap is a specialized tree-based data structure that satisfies the heap invariant: for every node $n$, the value of $n$ is less than or equal to (in a min-heap) or greater than or equal to (in a max-heap) the values of its children. In Java's java.util.PriorityQueue implementation, this logical tree is compressed into a flat, single-dimensional array. This design choice bypasses the pointer overhead and cache-miss penalties associated with node-and-pointer tree implementations, mapping parent-child relationships purely through index arithmetic.

items: Array Index Mapping: For any element at index $i$, its left child is located at $2i + 1$, its right child at $2i + 2$, and its parent at $\lfloor(i - 1) / 2\rfloor$. This implicit binary heap layout eliminates object header allocations for node wrappers.

Sift-Up (Percolate Up): When a new element is inserted, it is temporarily placed at the next available slot at the end of the array (the tail of the heap). To restore the heap invariant, the element is repeatedly swapped with its parent until the parent is smaller (or equal) or the root is reached.

Sift-Down (Percolate Down): During a poll operation (removal of the root), the last element in the array is moved to the root index. The algorithm then compares this element with its children, swapping it with the smaller child until the heap invariant is fully restored.

Dynamic Resizing: PriorityQueue starts with a default initial capacity (typically 11). When capacity is exhausted, its backing array grows via Arrays.copyOf, increasing capacity by approximately 50% for smaller arrays or 100% when arrays grow significantly larger.

parsed_answer.content: Production Gotcha: A PriorityQueue is NOT thread-safe. If multiple threads concurrently access a PriorityQueue, and at least one thread modifies the queue structurally, it must be synchronized externally or wrapped using java.util.concurrent.PriorityBlockingQueue. Furthermore, while poll(), offer(), and remove() operate in $O(\log N)$ time, bulk operations like contains(Object) or remove(Object) require a linear $O(N)$ scan because the underlying array is only partially ordered (the heap property guarantees parent-child ordering, but provides no sorted guarantees between sibling nodes).
